cultivar: Huangshan and Qimen landraces and standard clones; not cultivar-specific
processing: Fully pan-fired (chao qing) green: spring leaf is fired, rolled and dried in rotating pans until tightly twisted, then sorted by sieve into eyebrow-shaped grades such as Zhen Mei, Gong Xi and Xiu Mei.
harvest_season: Spring, from April into May for the main crop; blended across picking dates and gardens.
appearance_dry: Tight, twisted, slightly curved grey-green leaves with a dull sheen, graded by size.
appearance_wet: Even olive-green leaves, whole in the top grades.
taste_profile: Toasted rice and roasted chestnut with a brisk, slightly tart edge and a dry, honeyed sweetness; sturdy rather than delicate.

brewing.notes: Pot or gaiwan at 85 °C with slightly longer steeps than a bud tea; it is built for strength and takes a top-up well.

vintage_note: Sold year-round as a graded, blended green rather than by picking date: the historic Tunlü name covers the pan-fired eyebrow teas of the Huizhou counties, graded as Zhen Mei (Chun Mee), Gong Xi (Hyson), Xiu Mei and so on, with export numbers. A few domestic sellers now sell a 'special grade Tunlü' as a spring tea with a date. It keeps a year or more sealed.
description:
Tunlü, 'Tunxi green', is the collective name for the pan-fired greens of the old Huizhou tea counties in southern Anhui (Xiuning, Shexian, Yixian and the Tunxi district of Huangshan city), which were gathered, refined and shipped from the river town of Tunxi for the export trade. It was an important Chinese export green, and some of the Chun Mee, Hyson and gunpowder in Western and North African shops may well have started life as Tunlü.

The style is chao qing, fully pan-fired: the leaf is fired, rolled and then dried in rotating pans until it twists tight and dark, which fixes a toasty, durable character. The raw tea is then sorted by sieves and winnowers into eyebrow shapes and grades, the finest twisted leaf as Zhen Mei, the rounder as Gong Xi, the broken as Xiu Mei, each with export numbers.

In the cup it is a solid, warming green: toasted rice and roasted chestnut, a brisk, slightly tart edge and a dry honeyed sweetness. It is not refined and does not pretend to be; it brews strong in a pot at 85 °C and holds up to a top-up. As a Western-style afternoon green, brewed in a teapot for a couple of minutes, it is more satisfying than most delicate spring teas, which go thin treated that way.

Buying: traditional Tunlü is a graded commodity with no vintage, sold by grade name or number, and it keeps for a year or more sealed. A few Anhui sellers now market a premium spring 'special grade Tunlü' as a finer, fresher tea, which is worth trying if you want to see the style at its best. Otherwise, think of it as the honest everyday green behind many anonymous export labels.

If you enjoy the roasted side of it, Lao Zhu Da Fang from the same hills is the next step up in the same flavour family.
history:
Tunlü takes its name from Tunxi, the town in today's Huangshan city in southern Anhui, and it names a trade style more than a single garden tea. The full name, Tunxi green tea, was later shortened to the form used now.

It grew up beside Keemun in the same tea country, and the two are often named as a pair, Qi Hong and Tun Lü. Exact dates, firms and awards in its history are poorly documented, so none are given here.
